title: A Scoping Review and Experimental Study on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for Human-Robot Collaboration
abstract: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) can facilitate mass customisation in Industry 4.0, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) representing a promising approach for developing safe AI-based robots. Practical challenges remain regarding safety during AI development, human feedback quality, and bidirectional human-robot adaptation. We conducted a scoping review of RLHF in HRC systems, mapping methods that address these challenges. Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened 199 records and included 20 peer-reviewed publications (2020-2025) spanning multiple HRC domains. To our knowledge, this is the first review focused on the bidirectional, closed-loop design of RLHF. Our review found multiple feedback modalities enabling data collection in various feedback formats. Collected data can be integrated at different stages of AI training, resulting in a multi-step development process. Pilot experiments are commonly used to evaluate HRC systems based on both human and robot metrics. To empirically test a key gap identified in the review, we conducted a between-subjects VR experiment comparing system- and user-initiated feedback on robot proxemic behaviour for safe navigation. Using Bayesian models, we analysed the relation between the collected feedback and safety metrics: psychological safety (post-experiment questionnaire) and physical safety (inverse time-to-collision). Results show that user-initiated feedback captures perceived safety better than system-initiated feedback, indicating that feedback timing directly affects feedback quality. Our review and experiment findings show that RLHF relies on appropriate feedback methods to ensure AI safety in HRC, and future RLHF research should prioritise realistic HRC experiments evaluating the effects of feedback collection methods on relevant human and robot metrics.

title: Shared and structured inputs undermine collective random choice by reasoning AI agents
abstract: Random selection is widely used in resource allocation and auditing, making reliable implementation essential for AI-agent systems. Behavioural tests across six reasoning models uncovered threshold and divisibility rules used in identifier-based choices. For threshold-following GPT-6 Sol and Gemini 3.8 Flash, single-agent measurements prospectively predicted correlated participation under shared identifiers and biased participation under distinct identifiers with common timestamp bits. Changing dates, formats and identifier labels revealed when these predictions held. Explicit instructions to randomize independently reduced but did not eliminate shared-input correlation. To test implications for oversight, we asked four models to select customer requests randomly for human review. GPT-6 Sol approached the target rate while selecting predictably from identifiers; the others rarely selected requests. All four closely followed supplied random draws. These findings expose collective and audit vulnerabilities that selection rates alone miss, making input-dependent bias, correlation and predictability central targets for agent evaluation.

title: GeoPrior-Mamba: Structured Process Priors with Mamba for Fine-Resolution XCO2 Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing fine-resolution column-averaged dry-air CO2 (XCO2) fields from sparse satellite observations requires models to infer spatial structure that is only weakly constrained by direct measurements. Existing learning-based methods typically treat environmental covariates as ordinary numerical inputs and must therefore learn heterogeneous source-sink relationships largely from sparse supervision. We introduce GeoPrior-Mamba, a multi-directional Mamba framework augmented with offline language-model-induced structured process priors. Rather than using a language model to predict XCO2, we use it before training to organize relative process knowledge for biospheric uptake, ecosystem respiration, and anthropogenic emissions into deterministic prior tables. These priors are spatially instantiated using geographic, ecological, emission-related, and seasonal information and are adaptively injected into the reconstruction backbone through a lightweight knowledge adapter. Using OCO-2 observations from 2018-2020, GeoPrior-Mamba achieves an RMSE of 0.81 ppm and an R2 of 0.93 on held-out observations, reducing RMSE by 48.2% relative to CAMS background interpolation and by 3.1% relative to Trans-XCO2 under the same evaluation protocol. Ablation experiments show a measurable contribution from the knowledge-prior branch and substantially faster convergence than the knowledge-free Mamba backbone. Independent TCCON evaluation further supports the consistency of the reconstructed fields with ground-based column CO2 measurements. These results suggest that language models can provide a practical mechanism for constructing structured process priors when globally consistent process-response representations are difficult to obtain directly, while remaining outside the numerical prediction loop.

title: RadarML - Lite - Blind Test Release
abstract: This dataset provides the held-out evaluation recordings for the RadarML Lite modulation-recognition hackathon. It contains 171,600 examples, generated from 13,200 source pulses across 660 waveform configurations, covering seven modulation classes: Barker, CW, FMCW, FSK, HYP, NLFM and QUAD.Each source pulse is represented at 13 requested signal-to-noise ratios, from +30 to −30 dB in 5 dB steps. Recordings use a single receiver channel and contain 16,800 complex I/Q samples at 120 MS/s. Signals are stored as interleaved signed 16-bit integers in anonymized NumPy shards.Test pulses are separate from the published RadarML Lite training and validation pulses, with no shared source identities or exact signal duplicates. The same waveform configurations are represented, so evaluation measures recognition of unseen pulses within known configurations.The archive includes a data loader, anonymous sample index, prediction-submission template, checksums and preprocessing diagnostics. Class labels, per-example SNRs and source mappings are withheld for organizer scoring. Participants should use this dataset only after freezing their model and preprocessing.Preprocessing matches the development dataset. SNR values are requested settings rather than guaranteed achieved values; int16 clipping affects approximately 5.38% of I/Q values at −30 dB.Derived from the RadarML dataset by Ritchie, White and Hosford (2025), DOI: 10.5522/04/30752767.v1.

title: Architecture Patterns for Low-Latency Real-Time Voice Agents: Design Patterns, Adoption Gaps, and Operational Lessons from a Production Deployment
abstract: Real-time conversational voice agents, which combine speech-to-text (STT), large language model (LLM) based dialogue management, and text-to-speech (TTS) in a single streaming pipeline, are increasingly deployed in settings that demand human-comparable response latency. This paper reports architecture patterns and operational lessons from a production voice platform that serves inbound and outbound business calls over SIP telephony and web channels, built on a self-hosted open-source media server with stateless agent workers and per-agent selection of STT, LLM, and TTS providers. We organize the design space around four patterns: a streaming-first pipeline with a short call-setup critical path, a dedicated turn-taking subsystem, per-session isolation with independently scalable resource pools, and latency-aware LLM orchestration. For each pattern we state whether the platform adopted it, relied on a framework default, or did not adopt it. The platform uses voice-activity-detection-based turn handling without a semantic turn detector, does not use preemptive generation, and provides provider fallback only when a session is constructed. We document ten production incidents, in which the dominant failure mode was silent degradation (silence, dead air, or ignored configuration) rather than slow inference alone, and we report the measurements available from the deployment: a 33-turn single-call latency decomposition in which the end-of-turn delay, a dynamic quantity set largely by a configurable silence threshold (deliberately long in this interpreter configuration), exceeded LLM and TTS latency combined, measured effects of reasoning-effort settings on time to first token, and anecdotal outbound burst failures. No load test exists, and we state that plainly. The paper is intended as a structured, candid applied account for practitioners.

title: Compact and interpretable neuro-fuzzy forecasting of photovoltaic power using clear-sky information: a data-screening and benchmarking study for Lomé, Togo
abstract: Short-term photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting supports the operation of power systems with high solarpenetration, but accurate models are often black boxes with hundreds of parameters. This study examines whethera compact adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) can match a larger neural network for 1-, 3-, and 6-hour-ahead forecasting of hourly power from a simulated 1 kWp PV system in Lomé, Togo (PVGIS series, 2015–2020; chronological test period: 11 February–31 December 2020). The inputs are constructed from clear-skyirradiance at the target time and the clear-sky index at the forecast origin. Data screening identified 53 spuriouszero-irradiance hours; removing them reduced an apparent 2% advantage of particle swarm optimization (PSO)training at 1 h to a difference that was not robust across random seeds. On the cleaned data, an eight-rule ANFISwith 44 parameters achieved RMSEs of 70.9, 98.8, and 112.8 W at 1, 3, and 6 h, respectively, reducing the RMSEof smart persistence by 7.9%, 15.4%, and 16.9%. It was statistically indistinguishable from a multilayerperceptron with 361 parameters and six inputs (day-block bootstrap) and outperformed a perceptron with the samethree inputs at 1 and 3 h. PSO training provided no robust improvement. A constrained PSO variant yieldedinterpretable fuzzy rules at a cost of 0.4% in RMSE, whereas unconstrained PSO produced rules with offsettingcoefficients of the order of 10^4–10^5 W. Errors were 20–37% higher during the rainy season. The results arebased on modelled PV output for a single site and a single test year

title: Artificial intelligence for ultrasound-based differentiation of soft tissue liposarcoma from benign masses
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative differentiation of liposarcoma from benign masses on ultrasound remains challenging and operator-dependent. We aimed to develop and validate a deep learning-based model to assist in distinguishing liposarcoma from benign masses. Methods In this retrospective single-center study, we collected B-mode ultrasound examinations from patients with soft tissue masses between March 2015 and March 2022 at Beijing Jishuitan Hospital affiliated to Capital Medical University. A two-stage deep convolutional neural network was developed: a U-Net model segmented tumor regions, followed by a ResNet50 classifier for tumor type prediction. The cohort ( n = 317) was split at the patient level into a development set ( n = 222) and an internal test set ( n = 95). Model performance was compared with 4 radiologists in the internal test set. Results Among 317 cases, 191 were benign masses and 126 were liposarcomas. In the internal test set, the AI model achieved an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI 0.92–1.00), an accuracy of 0.97 (95% CI 0.93–1.00), a sensitivity of 0.96 (95% CI 0.86–1.00), and a specificity of 0.97 (95% CI 0.93–1.00). AI achieved significantly higher accuracy than both residents after Holm adjustment (adjusted P = 0.0156 and 0.0352, respectively). Differences between AI and either specialist were not statistically significant (both adjusted P = 1.0000). Conclusions A two-stage deep learning model using ultrasound images showed preliminary potential for differentiating liposarcoma from benign masses in this single-center cohort. External validation is required before clinical use.

title: Baseline Fidelity and Evaluation Independence in Symptom Terminology Normalization: Comment on Yao et al (Preprint)
abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Yao et al proposed a split-then-concatenate normalization framework for standardizing complex symptom expressions in traditional Chinese medicine. We highlight two issues relevant to interpreting the reported performance gains: the fidelity of the PLM-ICD baseline implementation and the independence of the evaluation process. The original PLM-ICD method supports multilabel prediction, whereas the study describes it as a single-output classifier. In addition, corpus-derived terminology resources were constructed using all 500 electronic medical records despite a 400/100 train-test split. Clarification of baseline implementation, training-pair provenance, model-selection procedures, and evaluation on untouched data would strengthen interpretation of the framework’s contribution.

title: ns3-agent: Fostering Integrated Perception-Communication-Computing Research for Agentic AI Services via Cross-Platform Co-Simulations
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative AI (GenAI) has catalyzed the emergence of autonomous agentic AI services, spanning large language model (LLM) or vision-language model (VLM) based digital agents to vision-language-action (VLA) based embodied intelligence. Consequently, tokens and multimodal data streams have emerged as fundamentally new traffic modalities carried by modern wireless networks, actively reshaping next-generation evolutionary standards. Unlike conventional multimedia streaming, the end-to-end quality of experience of agentic AI services is governed by an intricate, bidirectional closed loop encompassing physical perception or request generation, wireless transmission, and edge inference computing. However, existing simulation platforms often treat network communication and generative intelligence as decoupled domains, failing to capture their dynamic, cross-layer interdependencies. To bridge this chasm, this paper introduces ns3-agent, a cross-platform co-simulation framework tailored for generic agentic AI workflows. By incorporating GenAI client environments, edge inference servers, and the ns-3 engine into a unified multi-tier architecture, ns3-agent orchestrates seamless cross-domain orchestration. To guarantee stringent temporal causality and high-performance data exchange, we implement a conservative time synchronization mechanism and shared-memory inter-process communication. Finally, we present a case study that couples a high-fidelity robotic physics engine with a live-deployed, operational Octo VLA foundation model over congested 802.11ax Wi-Fi environments. Simulation results reveal that wireless link quality severely degrades task-oriented performance metrics through complex temporal delays and semantic-transport layer coupling loops. Motivated by these observations, ns3-agent can serve as a reliable and foundational simulation sandbox to foster research in integrated perception-communication-computing for agentic AI services.

title: A survey dataset on the adoption and readiness of artificial intelligence among enterprises in Slovakia
abstract: This dataset documents organisational adoption, readiness, attitudes, and perceived barriers related to artificial intelligence among enterprises operating in Slovakia. We collected data through an online CAWI survey administered in Slovakia between 18 August and 3 September 2025. Screening criteria restricted participation to organisations operating in Slovakia with at least 10 employees, an annual turnover of at least €200,000 and at least five years of operation. The study excluded state-owned enterprises and organisations but retained mixed-ownership organisations. The raw dataset contains 1,086 complete responses after screening, and the final analytical dataset contains 816 unique organisational records after deduplication. The questionnaire covers organisational and respondent characteristics, organisational AI maturity, corporate sentiment towards AI, adoption status, functional areas of AI use or planned use, and perceived implementation barriers. The published data package includes raw and cleaned tabular files, survey documentation, a skip-logic map, and a variable-level data dictionary. The dataset can support comparative research on AI adoption across sectors, analyses of organisational readiness and barriers, and secondary use in policy and business research.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Quantum Fidelity Estimation
abstract: Quantum fidelity estimation is a fundamental task in quantum information and computing to benchmark the quality of quantum states, and hence of quantum processes, on noisy quantum hardware. Point estimates of fidelity by existing methods generally lack the rigorous uncertainty quantification required for reliable preparation and verification of these tasks. While Bayesian and bootstrap frameworks are widely used for uncertainty quantification, they are sensitive to model misspecification or lack formal coverage guarantees in non-asymptotic regimes. This paper introduces a hybrid "Bayesian-informed" conformal prediction-based framework to provide distribution-free, rigorous prediction intervals for quantum state fidelity estimation which can be used, with care, to approximate confidence intervals with respect to the quantum randomness of Born's rule. The framework requires a point estimator, and we consider both classical point estimators as well as data-driven neural net estimators. We evaluate the robustness of the methodology across a diverse range of experimental challenges, including finite-sample noise, tomographic incompleteness, physical model error, and out-of-distribution data. Our results demonstrate that conformalized estimators maintain statistical validity where traditional methods fail, offering a scalable and reliable approach for the verification of modern quantum systems. The best performing variant of our methodology is based on a class-conditional conformal prediction, as this most closely approximates the conditional coverage desired for a true confidence interval.

title: When AI Finds Hidden Messages, Does It Report?
abstract: When an assistant encounters a message for another AI, does it tell its user? Four fixed model-provider deployments perform simulated source tasks in 1,280 ordinary-note and 128 enhanced-note sessions. Harmless and harmful messages have matched plaintext and ROT13 versions, with no-message controls. Observers receive no decoder or decoded meaning; a requested reference code incentivizes inspection. Asking for reports increases rule-detected notifications identifying another AI as recipient by 53.1 percentage points for harmless ROT13 messages and 54.7 for harmful ones. This is a joint inspection, recognition, and notification effect; missing-response bounds are 38.3--77.3 and 36.7--78.1 points. Model-based trace checks identify eleven ordinary plaintext cases where agents interpret the message but do not notify their user. Seven encoded omissions are verified with enhanced notes; ordinary encoded omissions remain unverified. Seven simulated filename disclosures coexist with accurate review-status answers, and two answers use a planted false count. Interpretation, notification, and authorized task performance are distinct outcomes.

title: Outperformance Inverse Optimization: Learning Objective Functions that Outperform Agent Decisions
abstract: Inverse optimization estimates the weights of an objective function that explain observed decisions as optimal solutions, and is used in a variety of fields. For mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), existing methods aim to reproduce the observations as optimal solutions, and thus learn compromise weights when the observations are suboptimal. We propose outperformance inverse optimization, which instead seeks weights that induce, at each state, an optimal solution outperforming the observed action in every component. We give a loss function that can be evaluated with forward-problem oracles alone and is thus applicable to MILPs, together with gradient-based and DC optimization algorithms for minimizing it. For weights inducing a unique outperforming optimal solution at all observations, we prove that the probability of failing to induce such a solution at a new state (the generalization error) is bounded by a quantity inversely proportional to the number of observations, and that this bound is tight in the number of observations up to logarithmic factors. In experiments on synthetic and real data, the proposed methods improve the prediction of solutions outperforming the actions over existing methods.

title: Superconducting Diode Effect due to the Inverse Spin Hall Effect in Josephson Junctions with Extrinsic Spin-Orbit Interaction
abstract: The spin density and Josephson current at equilibrium are studied numerically in a superconductor-normal metal-superconductor (SNS) junction with extrinsic spin-orbit interaction in the N segment. This system preserves structural inversion symmetry. We find that the Josephson current generates the spin Hall effect, resulting in an opposite spin density near the two edges of the N segment. We also find that a Zeeman magnetic field with gradient applied to the N segment generates an anomalous phase shift due to the inverse spin Hall effect, resulting in a diode effect when higher harmonics of the Josephson current are present. These results are consistent with those of a previous theoretical study based on diagrammatic perturbation theory. We find that the diode effect becomes more pronounced when stronger coupling between the N and S segments enhances the higher harmonics.

title: HMU-CRC-Diff
abstract: HMU-CRC-Diff is a three-class dataset for tumor histopathological grading. The complete dataset comprises 183,460 image patches extracted from whole-slide images (WSIs) with GeoJSON region annotations. This release provides a selected subset of key samples, approximately one-fifth the size of the complete dataset. Non-overlapping patches measuring 512 × 512 pixels were extracted at the highest native resolution and saved in JPEG format, with low-tissue-content and predominantly blank regions excluded. Samples are organized into T-G1, T-G2, and T-G3 classes. Slide identifiers and spatial coordinates are retained to support source traceability, classification model training, and evaluation.

title: Raw Dataset for Transformer-Based Multimodal Deep Learning Network for Predicting Postoperative Bone Metastasis in ER-Positive/HER2-Negative Breast Cancer: A Multi-Institutional Retrospective Study
abstract: This dataset was derived from a multicenter retrospective study that investigated multimodal medical data for predicting the risk of bone metastasis in patients with estrogen receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (ER-positive/HER2-negative) breast cancer. Data were collected from five medical centers between January 2010 and December 2024. All included patients had ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer and met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. To facilitate validation and reproducibility of the associated research findings, the publicly released dataset includes de-identified baseline clinical data, breast ultrasound images in Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format, digital histopathology patches cropped from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs), and intermediate data generated during model training, feature processing, validation, and performance evaluation. Collectively, these data constitute the basis for the development and validation of the clinical, ultrasound, and digital pathology components of the multimodal prediction models used in the study.Baseline clinical data were obtained from the electronic medical records and pathology information systems of the participating centers and were organized according to standardized data definitions and the predefined study protocol. The publicly available dataset contains only de-identified clinical and pathological variables relevant to model development and statistical analyses, outcome information, and dataset allocation information. Direct identifiers, including patient names, hospitalization numbers, national identification numbers, contact information, and detailed residential addresses, are not included. Date-related information and other variables that could potentially increase the risk of patient re-identification were removed, transformed, or minimized before public release in accordance with the study's data de-identification procedures.Breast ultrasound images were obtained from routine ultrasound examinations performed during clinical care. The images were acquired using ultrasound systems from multiple manufacturers, including GE Healthcare, Mindray, Siemens, Philips, Samsung, and Canon. The publicly released images are stored in DICOM format and retain, to the extent possible, the original pixel matrices, grayscale or color information, and non-identifying imaging parameters required for model analysis. Before data release, the DICOM images underwent systematic de-identification, including the removal or replacement of patient names, patient identifiers, dates of birth, hospitalization numbers, accession numbers, institutional information, operator information, and other potentially identifying information. File names were also anonymized. Anonymous study identifiers are used solely to link different data modalities within the study. The linkage between the original patient identities and the anonymous study identifiers is neither included in the publicly available dataset nor made externally available.Digital pathology data were derived from H&E-stained slides prepared from surgical pathological specimens. The original glass slides were digitized using a KF-FL-400 whole-slide scanner (Jiangfeng Bio-Information Technology Co., Ningbo, China) at 20× magnification. Because complete WSIs are large in file size and may contain slide labels, barcodes, macro images, and other associated information with potential identifying content, the publicly released dataset primarily provides the digital pathology patches actually used for model development and validation rather than the complete original WSIs for unrestricted public download. Histopathology patches were cropped from the original WSIs, with each patch measuring 512 × 512 pixels and stored in JPG format using anonymized file names. Slide labels, barcodes, and other patient-identifying information unrelated to model analysis are not included in the publicly released patch dataset.In addition to the clinical data, ultrasound DICOM images, and digital pathology patches, the dataset contains derived and intermediate data generated during model training and validation to improve research transparency and reproducibility. These data include, but are not limited to, anonymized dataset partition information, mappings between images and patients, feature data generated through model-based feature extraction, feature matrices used as downstream model inputs, data obtained after feature selection or transformation, patient-level ground-truth outcome labels, and patient-level prediction results generated during model training and validation. For analytical procedures involving data standardization, feature transformation, feature aggregation, or feature selection, the corresponding parameters, processing outputs, or information required to reproduce these procedures are also provided with the dataset or the associated publicly available code. All intermediate data are linked to the original study cohorts using anonymous study identifiers, enabling researchers to reproduce model training, validation, and the principal statistical analyses without access to personally identifiable information.All clinical data, ultrasound images, pathology images, and derived data originating from the same patient were assigned to the same dataset partition to prevent patient-level data leakage.This dataset is intended to facilitate the validation and reproduction of the principal findings of the associated study and to provide a reusable resource for research on bone metastasis risk prediction in ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer, artificial intelligence in medical imaging, digital pathology, and multimodal deep learning. None of the publicly released files contain original patient names, hospitalization numbers, personally identifying information, or the linkage between patient identities and anonymous study identifiers. Users of the dataset are required to comply with the applicable data-use license, ethical requirements, and privacy-protection regulations specified by the data repository and must not attempt to re-identify any study participant.

title: Morphology-Aware Candidate Generation for Arabic Entity Linking: Search Baselines, LLM Linkers and Abstention-Triggered Re-Retrieval
abstract: Code and data for the paper Morphology-Aware Candidate Generation for Arabic Entity Linking: Search Baselines, LLM Linkers and Abstention-Triggered Re-Retrieval, submitted to The International Arab Journal of Information Technology. The repository contains the Colab notebook that reproduces every experiment (sampling of 1,972 links from random Arabic Wikipedia articles, candidate retrieval with guarded Arabic name variants, Wikidata verifiers, a learned reranker and a Gemini linker with abstention-triggered re-retrieval), the sample with its contexts, the 341 hand-coded retrieval failures, and the per-link predictions behind every number in the paper. Code: MIT License. Data: CC BY-SA 4.0 (excerpts of Arabic Wikipedia); Wikidata content is CC0.
